two-sum.statement:
Given a list of integers `nums` and an integer `target`, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to `target`.

Exactly one pair works. You may not use the same element twice, and the two indices can come back in either order.

remove-duplicates-from-sorted-array.statement:
`nums` is sorted ascending and may repeat. Move the distinct values to the front, in order, and return `k` — how many there are.

The first `k` positions of `nums` must hold those distinct values when you return. Whatever is left beyond `k` does not matter. Do it in place: no second list.
constraints: The list is checked as well as the return value

best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock.statement:
`prices[i]` is the price of one share on day `i`. Buy on one day and sell on a later one. Return the largest profit available; if no day pair turns a profit, return `0`.

One buy and one sell — you cannot sell before you buy.

majority-element.statement:
Return the value that appears more than ⌊n/2⌋ times in `nums`.

You may assume such a value always exists, so there is no empty case to handle.

move-zeroes.statement:
Shift every `0` in `nums` to the end while the non-zero values keep their relative order.

In place — the list itself is what gets checked, not a copy you return.
constraints: Return nothing; the list is inspected afterwards

contains-duplicate.statement: Return `True` if any value appears at least twice in `nums`, and `False` if every element is distinct.

missing-number.statement: `nums` holds `n` distinct numbers drawn from the range `0..n` — so exactly one of that range is absent. Return it.
constraints: All values are distinct and in range `0..n`

plus-one.statement:
`digits` is a non-negative integer, one decimal digit per element, most significant first. Add one to it and return the digits of the result.

Mind the carry: `[9, 9]` becomes `[1, 0, 0]`, which is longer than it started.
constraints: No leading zeros, except the number 0 itself

merge-sorted-array.statement:
`nums1` has length `m + n`: `m` sorted values followed by `n` zeros to be written over. `nums2` holds `n` sorted values. Merge them so `nums1` ends up sorted.

In place, into `nums1`. Filling from the back is easier than from the front.

squares-of-a-sorted-array.statement:
`nums` is sorted ascending and may contain negatives. Return the squares of its values, sorted ascending.

Sorting afterwards works. Doing it in one pass from both ends is the point of the exercise.

intersection-of-two-arrays-ii.statement:
Return the values that appear in both `nums1` and `nums2`, keeping duplicates: a value present twice in one and three times in the other appears twice in the answer.

The order of the result does not matter — it is compared as a multiset.
constraints: Order of the result is not checked

rotate-array.statement:
Rotate `nums` to the right by `k` places, so the last `k` values wrap around to the front.

In place. `k` can be larger than the list.
constraints: Return nothing; the list is inspected afterwards

product-of-array-except-self.statement:
Return a list where each position holds the product of every value in `nums` except the one at that position.

Without division, and in linear time. Two passes — running products from the left, then from the right — get you there.
constraints: Every product fits in a 32-bit integer

maximum-subarray.statement:
Return the largest sum obtainable from a contiguous, non-empty run of `nums`.

All-negative input is allowed, in which case the answer is the least negative value.
constraints: The subarray must be contiguous and non-empty

sort-colors.statement:
`nums` holds only `0`, `1` and `2`. Sort it in place so the zeros come first, then the ones, then the twos.

One pass, no counting sort, no library sort — that is the exercise.
constraints: Return nothing; the list is inspected afterwards

subarray-sum-equals-k.statement:
Return how many contiguous subarrays of `nums` sum to `k`.

Negatives are allowed, so a sliding window will not do it. Running sums and a count of the ones already seen will.

find-the-duplicate-number.statement:
`nums` has `n + 1` values, each in the range `1..n`. By the pigeonhole principle at least one value repeats — and exactly one does. Return it.

Solvable without modifying the list and in constant extra space.
constraints: Exactly one value is repeated, possibly many times

3sum.statement:
Return every distinct triple of values from `nums` that sums to zero.

Distinct by value, not by index: `[-1, 0, 1]` belongs in the answer once, however many ways the list can produce it. Order does not matter, within a triple or between them — the judge compares them unordered.
constraints: Order is not checked, at either level

container-with-most-water.statement:
`height[i]` is the height of a vertical line at position `i`. Pick two lines so the container they form with the x-axis holds the most water, and return that area.

Area is the shorter of the two lines times the distance between them.

merge-intervals.statement: `intervals` is a list of `[start, end]` pairs. Merge every pair that overlaps or touches, and return the result sorted by start.
constraints: The result is sorted by start

set-matrix-zeroes.statement:
If any cell of the matrix is `0`, set its whole row and its whole column to `0`.

In place. The trap is doing it as you go: a zero you write is indistinguishable from a zero that was there, so the effect spreads.
constraints: Return nothing; the matrix is inspected afterwards

spiral-matrix.statement: Return every value of the matrix in spiral order — along the top row, down the right side, back along the bottom, up the left, then inward.
constraints: The matrix need not be square

next-permutation.statement:
Rearrange `nums` into the next permutation in lexicographic order. If it is already the largest, wrap around to the smallest — the sorted-ascending one.

In place, constant extra space.
constraints: Return nothing; the list is inspected afterwards

first-missing-positive.statement:
Return the smallest positive integer that does not appear in `nums`.

Linear time and constant extra space is the whole difficulty — which means using the list itself as the bookkeeping.

median-of-two-sorted-arrays.statement:
Two sorted lists, `nums1` and `nums2`. Return the median of the two combined.

Merging them is O(m + n) and will pass; the problem is really asking for the binary search on the shorter list.
constraints: A whole-number median comes back as a float, e.g. `2.0`

reverse-string.statement:
Reverse the list of characters `s` in place.

Constant extra space — two pointers walking towards each other, not a new list.
constraints: `s` is a list of one-character strings
Return nothing; the list is inspected afterwards

valid-palindrome.statement:
Return `True` if `s` reads the same forwards and backwards once you ignore case and drop everything that is not a letter or a digit.

An empty string, after that filtering, counts as a palindrome.
constraints: `s` may hold letters, digits, spaces and punctuation

valid-anagram.statement: Return `True` if `t` is an anagram of `s` — the same characters, the same number of each, in some order.

longest-common-prefix.statement: Return the longest string that every entry of `strs` starts with. If there is no common prefix, return `""`.

find-the-index-of-the-first-occurrence-i.statement:
Return the index of the first occurrence of `needle` in `haystack`, or `-1` if it does not occur.

An empty needle occurs at index `0`.

first-unique-character-in-a-string.statement: Return the index of the first character in `s` that appears exactly once, or `-1` if every character repeats.

isomorphic-strings.statement:
Return `True` if `s` and `t` are isomorphic: the characters of `s` can be replaced to get `t`, with each character mapping to exactly one other and no two characters mapping to the same one.

The mapping has to work both ways — that second half is what most first attempts miss.
constraints: A character may map to itself

ransom-note.statement: Return `True` if `ransomNote` can be built from the letters in `magazine`, each letter of the magazine usable at most once.

longest-substring-without-repeating-char.statement:
Return the length of the longest substring of `s` with no repeated character.

Substring, not subsequence — it has to be contiguous. A sliding window whose left edge jumps past the last sighting of the offending character does it in one pass.
constraints: `s` may hold letters, digits, symbols and spaces

longest-palindromic-substring.statement:
Return the longest palindromic substring of `s`.

Where two answers tie in length either is accepted only if the tests say so — here the expected answer is the one that starts earliest, so expand around each centre from left to right and keep the first of an equal-length pair.
constraints: On a tie, the earliest-starting substring is expected

group-anagrams.statement:
Group the entries of `strs` so that words which are anagrams of each other end up in the same list.

Order does not matter, within a group or between them — the judge compares them unordered.
constraints: Order is not checked, at either level

string-to-integer-atoi.statement:
Implement `atoi`: read a leading integer out of `s` the way C's function does.

Skip leading whitespace; take an optional `+` or `-`; read digits until a non-digit or the end; ignore everything after. No digits means `0`. Clamp the result to the 32-bit signed range, `−2³¹` to `2³¹ − 1`.
constraints: Clamp out-of-range results rather than wrapping them
Whitespace here means the space character

longest-repeating-character-replacement.statement:
You may change at most `k` characters of `s`, each to any uppercase letter. Return the length of the longest run of one repeated character you can produce.

A window is valid while its length minus the count of its most common character is at most `k`.

sort-characters-by-frequency.statement:
Return `s` rearranged so that characters appear in descending order of how often they occur, with all copies of a character together.

Characters that occur equally often are ordered by first appearance in `s`, which is what a stable sort of a counter gives you.
constraints: Letters and digits, upper and lower case

minimum-window-substring.statement:
Return the shortest substring of `s` that contains every character of `t`, counting duplicates. If there is none, return `""`.

Where two windows tie in length the earliest one is expected. Grow the window until it is valid, then shrink from the left while it stays valid.
constraints: `t` may repeat characters, and the counts must be met
Upper and lower case are different characters
On a tie, the earliest window is expected

contains-duplicate-ii.statement: Return `True` if `nums` holds two equal values whose indices are at most `k` apart.

word-pattern.statement:
`pattern` is a string of letters and `s` is a sentence of space-separated words. Return `True` if the words follow the pattern: each letter maps to exactly one word and each word to exactly one letter.

Like Isomorphic Strings, but over words — and the mapping has to hold both ways.
constraints: `s` has single spaces between words and none at either end

intersection-of-two-arrays.statement:
Return the values present in both `nums1` and `nums2`, each appearing once.

Unlike its sequel, duplicates are collapsed. The order of the result is not checked.
constraints: Each value appears at most once in the result
Order of the result is not checked

find-common-characters.statement:
Return the characters that appear in every string of `words`, including duplicates: a character present twice in all of them appears twice in the answer.

The order of the result is not checked.
constraints: Order of the result is not checked

unique-number-of-occurrences.statement: Count how many times each value occurs in `arr`. Return `True` if no two values occur the same number of times.

top-k-frequent-elements.statement:
Return the `k` values that occur most often in `nums`.

The order of the result is not checked. The answer is unique — no tie can straddle the cut-off.
constraints: Order of the result is not checked

longest-consecutive-sequence.statement:
Return the length of the longest run of consecutive integers that can be formed from the values in `nums`. They need not be adjacent in the list.

Linear time is the point: put the values in a set and start counting only from a value whose predecessor is absent, so each run is walked once.
constraints: The values need not be sorted

4sum-ii.statement:
Four lists of the same length. Return how many index quadruples `(i, j, k, l)` satisfy `nums1[i] + nums2[j] + nums3[k] + nums4[l] == 0`.

By indices, not by value, so repeated values are counted separately. Sum the first two lists into a counter, then look up the negation of each sum of the last two.

find-all-anagrams-in-a-string.statement:
Return the start index of every substring of `s` that is an anagram of `p`, in ascending order.

The windows are all the same length, so slide one of length `len(p)` and compare character counts as it moves.

4sum.statement:
Given a list of integers `nums` and an integer `target`, return every **unique** quadruplet `[a, b, c, d]` from `nums` that adds up to `target`.

The four values must come from four *different* positions, but they may repeat in value. No quadruplet may appear twice in your answer, and both the quadruplets and the numbers inside them can come back in any order.

Sort the list first: with the outer two numbers fixed by a pair of loops, the remaining two are found by walking a pointer in from each end.
constraints: The sum of four values can exceed 32 bits — Python integers do not overflow

count-subarrays-with-xor-k.statement:
Given a list of integers `nums` and an integer `k`, return how many **contiguous subarrays** have a bitwise XOR equal to `k`.

Counting every subarray directly is quadratic. Let `run` be the XOR of everything up to the current index: a subarray ending here XORs to `k` exactly when some earlier prefix XORed to `run ^ k`, so keeping a tally of the prefixes seen so far answers each position in constant time.

The empty prefix counts — start the tally with `{0: 1}`, or you will miss every subarray that starts at index 0.
constraints: Subarrays are contiguous; the empty subarray does not count

find-the-repeating-and-missing-number.statement:
A list `nums` of length `n` should hold every integer from `1` to `n` exactly once. One value appears **twice** and one is **missing**.

Return `[repeating, missing]`.

XOR everything in the list against every number from `1` to `n`: what survives is `repeating ^ missing`, since every other value cancels. Any set bit in that result is a bit on which the two numbers differ, so it splits both the list and the range into two groups — each containing exactly one of them.
constraints: Every value is between 1 and n
Exactly one value repeats and exactly one is missing
Solvable in O(n) time and O(1) extra space

count-inversions.statement:
An **inversion** is a pair of positions `i < j` where `nums[i] > nums[j]` — two elements that are in the wrong order relative to each other. Return how many inversions `nums` contains.

The count is a measure of how far the list is from sorted: already sorted gives 0, and fully reversed gives every pair.

Checking all pairs is quadratic. Count them during a merge sort instead: when the merge takes a value from the right half while `i` elements remain unused in the left, that value is smaller than every one of them, so it closes `i` inversions at once.
constraints: Equal values are not an inversion — the comparison is strict
